problem: Traditional cognitive architectures need many dedicated components and heavy engineered knowledge, while LLM-based robot agents struggle to bridge high-level language reasoning to low-level perception/control, maintain multi-step consistency, and learn from experience.
motivation: Flexible household robots need planning, execution monitoring, recovery and memory. LLMs show emergent reasoning, so it is worth testing to what extent an agentic LLM with tool calling and memory can serve as the core of a cognitive robot architecture, and where it fails (e.g. hallucinated success).
key_idea: Use a zero-shot function-calling LLM as the central reasoning core of a cognitive architecture, with a scratchpad as working memory, a ChromaDB episodic memory of self-written task reports, and high-level tools for perception, navigation, grasping and placement.
insight: LLMs can plan, sequence tools and replan from failure without explicit enforcement, but their hallucinated beliefs about task success undermine the episodic memory because memories are labelled with the agent's own belief; hence the memory effect is inconclusive (small gains for GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek, a small drop for Qwen on T2). Memory does reduce the number of tool calls on average (tool-call figure). The confusion matrices show all models except Claude overestimate success, and DeepSeek always believes it succeeded, so an external success verifier is needed.
method: Agentic LLM core: a function-calling LLM with chain-of-thought prompting receives all observations as text and decides plans, tool calls and replanning; nothing is explicitly enforced.

Tool interface: Look-Around, Move-To (A* on a semantic map), Grab, Place, each with text status and failure reasons from execution monitors, plus End-Task, Add-To-Scratchpad, View-Scratchpad, Search-Memory.
Working memory: the LLM context plus a scratchpad the agent writes to for plans and info that falls out of context.
Episodic memory: ChromaDB vector store of End-Task reports (task description, believed status, action summary), retrieved by semantic similarity via Search-Memory.

Simulated world: PyBullet two-room household (kitchen, living room, hallway) with an omnidirectional base and a KUKA iiwa 7-DOF arm; grasping is simplified to attaching the object when within a proximity threshold; perception is read from the simulator state, not vision.
Model set: GPT-4.1, Claude 4 Sonnet (APIs), Qwen3 Coder 480B (4-bit AWQ, vLLM), DeepSeek V3.1 (2-bit GGUF, llama.cpp).

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1, Claude 4 Sonnet (frozen APIs); Qwen3 Coder 480B A35B Instruct (4-bit AWQ) and DeepSeek V3.1 (2-bit GGUF) (frozen, locally hosted)
setting.model_size: Qwen3 Coder 480B (35B active); DeepSeek V3.1 quantised; GPT and Claude undisclosed
setting.training_data: none (training-free, zero-shot with episodic memory accumulated at test time)
setting.observation: text descriptions from simulator state (semantic-map location, nearby objects and their placement); no visual data
setting.action_space: high-level tool calls (Move-To semantic location, Grab object, Place at location, etc.)
setting.privileged: perception is read directly from the simulator state (GT object positions and types); grasping is simplified by attaching the object when close; ground-truth world state is used for evaluation only

numbers.extra: 84 executions; episodic memory accumulates up to 3
numbers.evidence: Tab. 1: Success rate on T1: GPT 100% (84 executions)

numbers.extra: 81 executions; T2 run only after T1 succeeded

numbers_note: Custom in-house simulated tasks only, no standard navigation benchmark. Memory-effect, tool-call and confusion-matrix results are given only in figures, so no numbers were extracted.
results: All four LLMs solve the placing task (T1) with 100% success, except Qwen at 80%. On the swap task (T2), success ranges from 44.4% (GPT-4.1) through 66.2% (Qwen) and 75.5% (DeepSeek) to 100% (Claude 4 Sonnet, but with 30–150 s latency per request). All models except Claude hallucinate success, and the effect of episodic memory on success is inconclusive, though it reduces tool calls.
limitations: Toy simulation with a static setup, text-only oracle perception and simplified grasping; no real robot and no comparison against other cognitive architectures.

Hallucinated success corrupts the episodic memory, and models refuse sequential tasks; Claude is too slow for a real robot; Claude has few runs (18/16) and the execution counts differ widely across models.
Only two tasks, and no baselines or ablation without memory beyond the incremental memory curves.
compares_to: Mon-Williams et al. 2025 (LLM code generation with a knowledge base)
